evidence: Read cold, instruction.md is a person asking for an app. Line 1: 'Can you build HireOps, the workspace our recruiting team lives in all day? ... Several of us have it open at once, so the hard part is that nobody's work gets trampled when someone else acts.' Lines 3-9 are first-person prose paragraphs giving needs with reasons ('I often move several candidates together; that has to be all of them or none', 'If a message arrives while I am reading further up, leave my place alone and just tell me there is something new'). There are no numbered or bulleted acceptance lists, no shall/must table and no feature matrix. Line 11 explicitly leaves 'layout and names are yours'; line 15 says 'How you lay the other files and routes out under /app is your call'. The only build-recipe-like content is lines 15-19: Node/Express/SQLite, node /app/server.js, port 3000/PORT, GET /api/health, /app/app.db/DB_PATH, seed path, accounts. That is the template-mandated runtime contract (quality-checks.md row 4 requires these facts to be stated), not an implementation recipe, and it sits after the product ask. Line 13 is the lesson-5 self-check sentence in requester voice ('please check it yourself the way we'll use it'). Lesson 12 check across every note file: grep for must/mustn't/shall/should across instruction.md and both notes found only instruction.md:3 'should say who', :5 'should show up', :9 'must never see', :15 'must start', 'mustn't depend', and hireops_rules.md:122 'should show up'. The notes have no 'must / must not' edge-case lists. hireops_rules.md is framed as 'the working rules our recruiting team follows' (line 3), and it says 'Routes, field names, element ids, button labels and the shape of the pages are up to you' (lines 3-5). Its strict edge cases carry user reasons: 'We like to know where a card was when it was rejected, because reopening takes it back to exactly that stage' (50-51); 'We're usually in the middle of something when an update lands, so...' (126-128); 'Some conversations run long, so one opens on its most recent 30 messages' (150); 'Candidates are outside the company, so nothing their browser receives may contain...' (199-201); 'Our servers don't always start Node from inside the app folder...' (206-210). The two tables (role purposes, lines 15-20; candidate wording, 190-197) are domain reference data a real team would hand over, not acceptance matrices. The criteria (44 functional, 5 polish, 5 visual) cover topics described in the rules, but the rules are not phrased as one bullet per criterion. They do not repeat criterion phrasing, such as the controls, the 'Fails if' clauses or the replay setup. Instances checked for 'telling the builder how to build so the grader can test it' (lesson 12): (a) HTTP statuses 401/403/404/409 (rules 22-24, 80) are an API contract, and each has a user-facing reason: '404, so they can't even learn that it's there', and for 409, 'the refusal itself says the card was changed and by whom, so whatever screen or tool sent the move can tell them'. (b) 'every card carries a version that changes whenever the card moves' (78) is light implementation phrasing with a stated reason ('Several of us work the same board'); no criterion grades a version field, because hro_stale_refused grades the outcome. (c) 'Polling, server-sent events and sockets are all fine' and 'Where drafts are kept is up to you' widen freedom rather than prescribing. None turns the prompt into a spec sheet or build recipe. Counterexample attempt: no plausible model behavior or conforming app is mis-graded by this row's wording; the row concerns prompt naturalness, not app behavior, so the broken-app and conforming-alternative probes do not apply. Runtime evidence is not required for this judgement row. Minor non-blocking observations, not defects: the status-code sentences and the 'so whatever screen or tool sent the move' clause are the most spec-flavoured lines and could be softened if a portal reviewer is strict, but they are reasoned and sparse.
